chapter_theme: The description of Rajamapuram continues: the engines on its wall and the wall as a maiden, the heaven-like inner city, the courtesans' quarter where kings linger, the crowded market of honest merchants, the many-sided streets, and the start of the houses; praise of wealth and pleasure is set out without judgement, with one hint (kings held by desire) that the story will take up.

cast.role: foreign craftsmen who built and set the wall's engines
the courtesans of Rajamapuram's pleasure quarter
the courtesans' maids who carry messages and name prices
kings and princes who visit the courtesans' quarter
the merchants of the market streets
people bearing offerings in the streets
the young men of the city streets
the women of the city's streets and houses

102.reading: The narrator lists the engines mounted on the city wall: bow-machines, released horses, chained spears and swords, stone-throwers, figures, swans, fire-pots, killing brands, great cranes and owls, and devices that twist off heads and crush.
102.nuance: Many of the names are of devices whose working the verse does not explain; the list is read item by item and some items (பாவை, அனம், கூகை) may be shapes given to engines rather than separate machines.

103.reading: The engines, set in place by the Yavanas with their own skills, turn every way and spit molten copper, red-hot balls, boiling ghee, arrows, spears and stones.
103.nuance: The defence is credited to foreign craftsmen and to machines, not to the city's own fighting men; the wall is shown as self-acting, which is worth holding against how the city is later lost from inside.

104.reading: Iron boars, carts that let loose angry snakes, fighting monkeys and rams and cutters of fine thread stand with gold flags and banners, set so that enemies' heads tremble.
104.nuance: The verse ends the wall-catalogue on the enemy's fear (தெவ்வர் தலை பனிப்ப): the engines are meant to deter as much as to kill.

105.reading: The wall is pictured as a maiden: its diamond-bolted gate is her face, its bastions her breasts, its gold banners her hair and its moat her garment, rising like a mountain that opens its eyes among the clouds.
105.nuance: கன்னி makes the conceit pointed: the wall is an unwed girl, a fortress never taken, and the comparison praises beauty and impregnability in one figure.

106.reading: The narrator turns to the inner city, whose families scatter gold like rain at every step, bring treasure from the gold-yielding islands and feed many, and says it is like the world of the gods before telling a little of it.
106.nuance: The wealth is overseas trade wealth (பைம் பொன் விளை தீவில் நிதி), and its use is given at once: பலர்க்கு ஆர்த்தி, filling many. Praise of riches is tied to sharing in the same line.

107.reading: The narrator announces the quarter of the courtesans, whose coral-lipped maids carry love's messages and name a price from one up to a thousand and eight, and who sell their beauty without limit.
107.nuance: வரைவின்றி, 'without limit', is the same word that names the Kural's chapter on such women (வரைவின் மகளிர்). The epic uses it in a passage of praise. The sense of உப்பு அமை காமத் துப்பின் (love's relish, seasoned with salt) is not certain.

108.reading: Their houses have floors smeared with saffron, inlaid platforms and seats, hanging sandal-paste and garlands, plays painted on every wall and beds strewn with soft flowers, a delight like heaven's.

109.reading: Their courtyards are strewn with pearl girdles dropped because the hips could not bear them, sandal rubbed from breasts, scented powders and garlands for the bees, and their fragrance holds kings who linger there in desire.
109.nuance: ஆசைப் பட்டு அரசு வைக is the one note in the catalogue that points beyond ornament: kings stay because they desire. The book's own king will soon be warned that a king given to women's pleasure earns sin and blame.

110.reading: The sounds of anklets, girdles, hand-beats keeping time to song, flutes, and drums that never sleep make the quarter something heaven cannot equal.

111.reading: Incense from honeyed garlands veils the stars and makes night in the great city while the women's jewels pour moonlight and make day; the street that the god of spring desires is like the upper world.
111.nuance: வேனிலான் is Kama, the god of the spring season; the quarter is his chosen street, and the verse ends by calling it heaven's equal, the third such comparison in five verses (106, 110, 111).

112.reading: The narrator says he will now describe the market, laid out by the rule-book without fault, a yojana long, its squares loud with crowds and bright with silks, gold ornaments and men in honeyed garlands.
112.nuance: இட்ட நூல் வழாமை: the town is built by a treatise of town-planning. The narrator speaks in the first person singular here (உற்றேன்) and the plural elsewhere (உரைப்பாம், மொழிவாம்).

113.reading: The merchants set up their shops with gold knobs, strings of pearl, coral posts and screens, smear the floor with sandal, burn agil and scatter gold flowers and fragrant white mustard.
113.nuance: ஐயவி, white mustard, is scattered for good fortune: the shop is readied like a shrine.

114.reading: They open the gold-bolted Yavana chests and heap up gems, pearls and diamonds, then piles of coral and of white ornaments, and pile the fine pieces that make night at noon.
114.nuance: நண் பகல் இரவு செய்யும் inverts verse 111, where jewels make day of night; here a heap of jewels is said to make night at midday, perhaps by dark stones. The sense is not certain.

115.reading: They are men whose conduct is not to pick up the costly ornaments that fall and scatter, their wealth is past telling, and at every shop they set up areca, coconut and plantain trees with fruit made of gold and gems.
115.nuance: The honesty is given as their own ஒழுக்கம் (conduct) amid surfeit, with no guard, punishment or spirit to enforce it.

116.reading: The crowd hums like bees at the hive or the beating waves, so that only noise is heard and no word can be made out, sandal smeared on one man is rubbed onto seven, and the great throng has no room.

117.reading: Gold powder and perfumed water wash down and mix with the musth of elephants into mire, ornaments, garlands and toddy lie thick, and no one can set a foot down hot; the narrator turns to the streets.

118.reading: On one side the old drum-adorned city sounds with drums and conchs, festival women's young breasts breathe fragrance, their jewels shine like the early sun, and the smoke they release hides all like cloud.

119.reading: On another side umbrellas jostle umbrellas and tuskers press, worshippers go with offerings amid a roar like the sea, and crowns press so close that their light flickers like lightning in a bannered cloud.
119.nuance: பலி, the offering, is the one sign of worship in the street scenes; the kings' crowns and the worshippers share the press.

120.reading: On another side young men who fight crested cocks call out with folded tongues amid dancing and cuckoo-like song, and the place is thick with gold dust and fragrant pollen.
120.nuance: நாத் தலை மடி விளி is read as a whistling call made with the tongue folded; the reading is not sure.

121.reading: On another side young men seize the fine garments of women who are sulking with their lovers, so that girdle beads break and spill on the floor and shine like Indra's bow.
121.nuance: The ஊடல் of love-poetry becomes a street sight: the broken girdle, a sign of the lovers' quarrel ending, is valued for its rainbow.

122.reading: On another side rings out the call: here is rice like cut conch, ghee without measure, curried relish and set curd, eat and hurry, there are fine dishes.
122.nuance: The verse gives only the words of the call (உரை), not who calls; it may be householders feeding comers or sellers of food. The insistence (மிசை குவிர் விரையுமின்) is the hospitality formula, so it is tagged virundhu with that doubt.

123.reading: On another side the street is like a cold, roaring river, where tuskers shed musth like falls from a mountain range and pour along with jewelled chariots, swift horses and young men mingled.

124.reading: The narrator says he will tell properly of the fine houses, beautiful with the noise of bangles, of jewelled drums and of the ornaments of women with streaked eyes, along with the flute.

125.reading: When girls like dolls strike their balls, a swan takes fright, flies to the pearl-hung terraces taking the white moon for its mate, and settles beside it.
125.nuance: The catalogue of the house begins with a small error of perception: the bird mistakes the moon for a swan, as the city everywhere is made to rival heaven.

links.note: The Cintamani's wall is armed by Yavana engines that throw molten metal, arrows and stones outward; Kural 747 names three ways a fort is taken, the third (அறைப்படுத்தல்) by working on those inside.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show that the epic's elaborate machinery answers only the outward assaults of the couplet's list, leaving the inside danger by which this city is in fact lost to its own minister.

gains.a: the engine catalogue acquires an ironic edge, since the couplet names the threat no machine can meet
gains.b: the couplet's abstract third danger gets a concrete case of a fully armed city whose defences all face outward

links.note: Both use வரைவு for the courtesans: the epic says they sell beauty வரைவின்றி, the Kural calls such women வரைவிலா and their arms a mire for base men.
links.teaches: The same word that the Kural uses to condemn the courtesan becomes in the Jain epic an item in a city's praise, so the reader sees that a heaven-like city could include the trade the ethical book calls a hell.

gains.a: the epic's praise is shown to carry a word the ethical tradition had already loaded with blame
gains.b: the couplet's condemnation is set against a poem that celebrates the same openness as wealth and beauty

links.note: Verse 109 has kings linger in the courtesans' quarter out of desire; at 206 a counsellor warns the king that many who gorged on women's pleasure fell into sin and blame.
links.teaches: The pleasure that the city praise lets kings enjoy without comment is the same pleasure that the story will turn into a warning to its own king, so the description quietly prepares the charge.

links.note: Both cities leave goods unguarded: Puhar's open court keeps bundles safe because a spirit punishes the thief, the Cintamani's merchants leave fallen jewels lying as a matter of their own conduct.
links.teaches: The pair gives two different accounts of why a rich city's goods are safe, one by fear of a guardian spirit's punishment and one by the citizens' surfeit and habit, so honesty is shown as either enforced or assumed.

links.note: The Silappathikaram opens its Puhar with the earth as a woman, sea for garment, hills for breasts, rivers for hair; the Cintamani makes the city wall a maiden with the moat for garment and bastions for breasts.
links.teaches: The same body-map moves from the whole earth to a single wall, and the Cintamani's word கன்னி turns it into a figure of a fortress never entered, which the Silappathikaram's earth-woman does not carry.

links.note: Kural 215 likens the wise man's wealth to a full village tank everyone draws from; verse 106 has the inner city's families bring wealth from overseas islands and feed many (பலர்க்கு ஆர்த்தி).
links.teaches: The couplet says shared wealth is like a common tank but not where it comes from; the epic supplies the source in perilous sea trade and makes feeding many the mark that justifies calling the city heavenly.

gains.a: the epic's praise of wealth is given an ethical test, that the wealth is used to fill many
gains.b: the couplet's image of a public tank gains a whole merchant class acting it out
